title: Spinoza's calm
hook: Spinoza, not a Stoic, also taught that understanding our emotions' causes makes us freer (Ethics 5)

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Neostoicism, Lipsius writing through Europe's religious wars. Your line was constancy: steadiness built in here, not out there.

Holland, the 1660s. A man sits at a bench grinding glass lenses for microscopes and telescopes, slow work, where a rushed hand ruins the piece. Alongside the lenses, he is writing a book laid out like a geometry textbook: definitions, axioms, propositions, proofs. It's about God, nature and the human mind, and its last part is about something very ordinary: how to be a little less pushed around by your own feelings. His name is Baruch Spinoza. He wasn't a Stoic, and he said so. But today he sits on the porch's front step.
screen: `HOLLAND, A LENS GRINDER'S BENCH.` → `A BOOK BUILT LIKE GEOMETRY.` → `NOT A STOIC, BUT CLOSE BY.`

segments.voice: First, the book. Spinoza's Ethics was published in 1677, the year he died. Its fourth part is titled, in the old English translations, Of Human Bondage: being dragged along by passions you don't understand. The fifth part is about freedom. Second, the idea. Early in part five, Spinoza argues that a feeling which is a passion, something that just happens to us, stops being a passion once we form a clear and distinct idea of it. Put plainly: understand a feeling's causes, and it has less hold on you. Not because you crushed it, but because you saw it. Anger at your sister turns out to be tiredness, an old childhood hurt and a missed lunch, all at once. Seen whole, it shrinks to its real size. Third, where he parts from the Stoics. In the preface to that same part, Spinoza names them. The Stoics, he says, thought our feelings depend entirely on our will, so we could command them completely, though even they had to admit it takes long practice. For Spinoza, the will alone isn't the tool. Understanding is. So he's a neighbor, not a member: close to Epictetus's idea that our judgments disturb us, but built on different ground. Fourth, why it helps on a Tuesday. You can't always change a feeling by deciding to. But you can almost always get curious about it. Curiosity is a kind of distance, and a little distance is a kind of freedom.
screen: `ETHICS, 1677: BONDAGE, THEN FREEDOM.` · `SEE A FEELING'S CAUSE, IT LOOSENS.` · `NOT WILLPOWER: UNDERSTANDING.` · `CURIOSITY IS A KIND OF DISTANCE.` · then, large: `UNDERSTAND IT.`

segments.voice: Pick one feeling that's been with you today, irritation, worry, a low hum of sadness, and name it without trying to get rid of it. Ask slowly where it came from, and let a few causes show up, something someone said, how you slept, something older than today, laid out like lenses on a bench. Notice whether the feeling changes size as you look; if it doesn't, that's fine too.
Spinoza's calm: not a feeling switched off, but a feeling understood, its causes seen clearly, so it pushes you around a little less. Today's word.
Your line: understand it. A feeling seen whole pushes a little less. That's day six hundred sixty-two.

howItsDone: Readers of Spinoza often treat a strong emotion as something to understand rather than fight, tracing its causes until it loosens its grip.

notes: Ethics 5 prop. 3 paraphrased (an emotion which is a passion ceases to be a passion as soon as we form a clear and distinct idea of it). Confirm.

Ethics 5 preface: Spinoza says the Stoics thought emotions depend absolutely on our will and we can command them absolutely, but that experience forced them to admit much practice is needed. Confirm the paraphrase.
Part 4 title 'Of Human Bondage' follows the Elwes (1883) English rendering; Latin 'De Servitute Humana'.
Spinoza ground lenses for a living (commonly reported); in the 1660s he lived in Rijnsburg and Voorburg, later The Hague; hook says Holland.
Ethics published posthumously in 1677 (Opera Posthuma). Confirm.
Reviewer edit: the teach now says the Stoics themselves admitted long practice was needed (as in the preface), rather than presenting that as Spinoza's counter-argument.
How much Spinoza owed to Stoicism is debated by scholars; the script says only that he named and criticized them. Confirm 'he said so' is fair.
